channel.title: Thirsty Planet
channel.description: Understanding water, before it's gone. The hidden water inside everyday things, the water industry in plain words, and the places already solving it.

item.title: Thirsty: Salmon
item.description:
A farmed salmon carries about two thousand litres of water per kilogram, and almost none of it is the water it swam in. Seawater in a fjord in Norway or Chile is counted at nothing, because nobody else could use it and the fish does not consume it. The water is in the feed: the soy from Brazil, the wheat from Europe, the rapeseed oil and the fishmeal that make up the pellets a salmon eats for three years, at a little over a kilogram of feed for every kilogram of fish.
That puts salmon close to chicken and far below beef, and it makes salmon the animal on this site whose water is furthest from the animal. The fjord is clean, cold and free. The soybean field is in Mato Grosso, on rain and on land that was forest.
The fresh water is at the beginning. A salmon is hatched and grown to a hundred grams in fresh water, in tanks fed from rivers and lakes, and the newer hatcheries recirculate almost all of it. The industry's next move, driven by sea lice and escapes, is to keep the fish on land for its whole life, in tanks that need water, power and a pump, and that is where the fresh water number will grow.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Johannesburg
item.description:
Johannesburg is the largest city in the world that was not built on a river, a lake or a coast. It sits on the Witwatersrand, the ridge where the gold was found in 1886, and every litre it drinks is pumped about three hundred metres uphill from the Vaal river, seventy kilometres to the south. The Vaal, in turn, is fed by tunnels through the Maluti mountains from dams in Lesotho, a separate country, under a treaty signed in 1986.
In 2024 the dams were full and the taps ran dry. Suburbs across the city went for days without water, hospitals brought in tankers, and the cause was the last twenty kilometres: pumps that failed in a heatwave, reservoirs that emptied because the pipes below them leaked close to half of what went in, and a utility that had stopped replacing what it could not afford to maintain. The water was there. The system that delivers it had been allowed to fail.
The gold mines that made the city are the other story. Their tunnels are filling with water that turns to acid on the pyrite, and it rises toward the surface of the ridge the city sits on.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Dhaka
item.description:
Dhaka gets two metres of rain a year and sits on the largest river delta on Earth, and it drinks from wells. About two thirds of the water the city's utility supplies is pumped from the ground by close to a thousand deep wells, and the water table under the city has been falling by two or three metres a year for forty years. It is now sixty or seventy metres down in the centre, in a city that was built on a floodplain a few metres above the sea.
The reason is the rivers. The Buriganga, the Turag, the Balu and the Shitalakshya ring the city, and for most of the year they carry its sewage, the effluent of thousands of dye houses and, until 2017, the chrome of the tanneries at Hazaribagh, at concentrations that leave them black and without oxygen through the dry season. A city surrounded by water had nothing it could treat, so it drilled.
The wells cannot go on. The utility is building large plants on the cleaner rivers upstream, and the plan is to reverse the ratio, two thirds from the surface by the 2030s. It depends on the rivers being brought back to something a treatment works can take.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Athens
item.description:
Athens gets less rain than London by a wide margin and in some years less than Tunis, and it has never had a river to drink from. For fifteen centuries it drank from an aqueduct the Roman emperor Hadrian had dug under the city, and the aqueduct still runs. In the twentieth century it built a dam at Marathon and a pipe to a lake, and when those ran short it dammed a river in the mountains two hundred kilometres to the west and built the longest aqueduct in Europe to bring the water to the city.
In 1990 the reservoirs fell so low that the city rationed by district and the government considered tankers from the Rhine. In 2024, after two dry winters, the reservoirs were at their lowest in thirty years and the utility began pumping from the underground lake of Yliki and from wells that it had kept as reserves. The dry years that used to come once a decade are coming closer together.
The city's newest answer is its oldest. The aqueduct of Hadrian, which carries water it cannot drink, is being reopened to water the parks so that the reservoir water is kept for the taps.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Orange Juice
item.description:
A litre of orange juice carries about a thousand litres of water, and a glass about two hundred. The fruit carries about 560 a kilogram, and the juice carries roughly twice that because a kilogram of oranges gives about half a kilogram of juice and the water follows the juice. The peel, the pulp and the seeds go to cattle feed and the water goes with the juice.
Most of it is in one place. The state of São Paulo in Brazil grows about a third of the world's oranges and makes about three quarters of the orange juice that is traded, most of it as frozen concentrate shipped in tankers to Europe and the United States and reconstituted there. The groves are mostly rain fed, on a plateau with a wet summer, and the number is mostly green. Florida, which was the other half of the world's supply in 2000, has lost about ninety percent of its crop to a bacterial disease carried by an insect, and grows little now.
The Spanish and Californian oranges that are sold as fruit are the irrigated ones, on wells and rivers in the driest parts of both places, and their water is the water this site counts as somebody else's.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Slaughterhouses
item.description:
A slaughterhouse uses about ten cubic metres of water for every tonne of carcass it produces, and a chicken plant about twenty litres a bird. Against the fifteen thousand litres that the beef article on this site counts for a kilogram of beef, that is nothing. Against a river, it is a great deal, because what leaves the plant is among the strongest effluents in the food industry.
The water goes into washing: the animal before, the carcass after, the floors, the knives, the hooks and the chill tanks, all of it hot, all of it with chlorine or detergent, and all of it continuously, because the rule of the plant is that nothing touches meat twice without being washed. What comes out carries blood, fat, paunch contents, manure and the wash water, and a litre of blood has an oxygen demand of a hundred and fifty grams, which is three hundred times raw sewage.
The plants that work catch the blood, render the fat and treat the rest. The ones that do not send out a river's worth of oxygen demand from a single building.
The long version is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Hotels and Tourism
item.description:
A hotel guest uses about three hundred litres of water a night in an ordinary hotel and up to two thousand in a resort with pools, lawns, a spa and a golf course. The person who lives in the town outside the gate uses about a hundred and fifty. The difference is the pool, the laundry, the garden and the fact that nobody on holiday takes a four minute shower.
Tourism's water problem is where and when. The industry is largest on the coasts and islands with the least rain, and its season is the dry one, so that on Mallorca, Crete, Rhodes and the Canaries the population doubles or triples in the months when the aquifers are lowest, and the wells that supply the hotels pull seawater in behind them. The islands have answered with desalination, paid for by the hotels and run for the summer, and with the reuse of the resorts' own effluent on their gardens.
The golf course is the extreme case. A course in a dry climate drinks the water of a town of ten thousand people, and the coasts of southern Spain have hundreds.
The long version is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Groundwater
item.description:
Of all the fresh water on Earth that is liquid and not in a lake, about ninety nine percent is underground, in the pores of sand, gravel and rock. The world pumps about a thousand cubic kilometres of it a year, roughly a third of everything it uses and about half of what it drinks, and the largest user by far is irrigation. India pumps a quarter of the total on its own, from twenty million wells.
Groundwater fills slowly, from rain that soaks through the soil, and in the dry regions where it is pumped hardest it fills at a fraction of the rate it is drawn. The satellites that measure the Earth's gravity have watched the water table fall across northern India, the North China Plain, the Central Valley of California, the American plains, the Middle East and the Murray Darling since 2002, and the fall is the difference between what goes in and what comes out.
A well is a loan against a stock that took thousands of years to fill. Some of the stock, in the Sahara and under the Arabian peninsula, is fossil water that fell as rain before the last ice age and will never be replaced. Most of the wells on Earth are on a loan of that kind and nobody is counting.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Chlorine Byproducts
item.description:
In 1974 a Dutch chemist and an American one, working separately, found chloroform in tap water, and worked out where it came from: the chlorine added at the works was reacting with the traces of dissolved leaf and soil in the river water to make it. Every chlorinated supply in the world had it, at tens of micrograms a litre, and had had since chlorination began in 1908.
The compounds are called trihalomethanes, and with their cousins the haloacetic acids they are now regulated everywhere, at a hundred micrograms a litre in Europe and eighty in the United States. The evidence that matters is from bladder cancer: long term studies find a small increase in risk in people who have drunk chlorinated water with high byproduct levels for decades, and the regulators have set the limits to hold that risk down.
The answer was never to stop chlorinating. It is to take the organic matter out before the chlorine goes in, which is what coagulation and carbon do, and to add the chlorine last, at the lowest dose that holds through the pipes. The cholera that chlorine stopped killed more people in a year than the byproducts could in a century.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Myth: Water from the Hot Tap Is Fine to Drink
item.description:
The cold tap in a kitchen is connected to the mains, and the water in it is what the utility treated and tested. The hot tap is connected to a tank or a heater in the house, and the water in it has sat in a vessel at fifty or sixty degrees, in contact with the tank's lining, its sediment, its sacrificial anode and every metre of copper, brass and, in an old house, lead between the tank and the tap. Hot water dissolves metal faster than cold. The utilities say to drink and cook from the cold tap, and the reason is the pipe rather than the heat.
The myth is that water is water and the hot tap is a shortcut to the boil. It is a shortcut to whatever the plumbing is shedding. The advice is a century old, from the era of lead pipes and cistern fed hot systems, and in a new house with plastic pipe and a combination boiler the difference is small. In an old one it is a real difference, and nobody can tell from the tap which house they are in.
The second reason is the tank. Water held between twenty five and forty five degrees grows Legionella, and a tank kept too cool to save energy is a warm, still, nutrient rich vessel with a shower on the end of it.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFacts #WaterEducation #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Sunflower Oil
item.description:
A kilogram of sunflower oil carries about 6,800 litres of water. The seed carries about 3,400, and the oil is twice that because a kilogram of seed gives less than half a kilogram of oil, and the water follows the oil. Olive oil is 14,500. Rapeseed is 4,300. Palm oil is about 5,000, and the argument about palm oil is about land, not water.
Almost all of the sunflower's water is rain. The crop grows on the steppe of Ukraine and southern Russia, on the plains of Argentina and in the dry summers of southern Europe, with a tap root that goes two metres down and finds water that a shallower crop misses. It is rarely irrigated and it is one of the least thirsty oils on this site, in the water that anyone else could have had.
The war in Ukraine in 2022 took half the world's sunflower oil exports off the market in a month and put rationing signs on supermarket shelves in Europe. The water was never the problem. The port was.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Sydney
item.description:
Sydney drinks from one dam. Warragamba, on the Nepean west of the city, holds about two thousand billion litres and supplies four fifths of five million people. When it is full, the city has three or four years of water in it. When it fell to a third in the drought of 2007, the state government ordered a desalination plant, and when the rains came in 2010 and filled the dam the plant was switched off and sat idle for seven years.
In 2019 the dam fell again, faster than it ever had, and the plant was switched back on. It runs at 250 million litres a day, about fifteen percent of the city's use, and the government has now decided to double it. The critics said a plant that sits idle for years is a waste. The engineers said a plant that sits idle for years is insurance, and insurance is exactly what a city with one dam needs.
Sydney is the city on this site that shows how the choice between a dam and a desalination plant plays out over twenty years. The answer was both: a dam for the ordinary years and a plant for the ones the dam cannot cover.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Nairobi
item.description:
Nairobi needs about 800,000 cubic metres of water a day and gets about 500,000. The difference is managed by rota: every district of the city has its water turned off for part of every week, and has had since 2017, when a drought emptied the Ndakaini dam and the utility decided the schedule was permanent. Of the 500,000 that enter the pipes, close to half leak out or are never paid for.
The people who pay most are the people with no pipe. In Kibera and Mathare, the informal settlements that hold a third of the city, water comes from kiosks and vendors at a few shillings a jerry can, which works out at five to ten times what a household in a wealthy suburb pays per litre for water from its own tap, and it runs out when the rota turns the mains off upstream.
The fix, twenty years in the planning, is a tunnel under the Aberdare hills that brings three rivers into the city's dam. It opened, in stages, from 2022. It adds about a quarter to the supply, and the city grows by about that much each decade.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Istanbul
item.description:
Istanbul sits on the Bosphorus with the Black Sea at one end and the Marmara at the other, and it is short of water. In January 2021 its reservoirs fell to a fifth, the lowest in fifteen years, and the utility said publicly that the city had about forty five days of supply left. Prayers for rain were said in the mosques. Then it rained, and the crisis passed, and the reason for it did not.
The reason is growth. Istanbul had a million people in 1950 and has sixteen million now, and it has outgrown every reservoir built for it: Terkos in the 1880s, Ömerli in the 1970s, a pipe from the Melen river two hundred kilometres to the east in the 2010s. Each was the answer for a decade. The city's rain falls mostly in winter, its reservoirs are shallow and its catchments are being built over, and in a dry winter the arithmetic runs out. Each reservoir was the answer for a decade, and each decade the city grew past it.
The Melen dam, which was meant to finish the job, cracked during construction and was years late. It is the city's insurance and it is not yet fully in place.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Semiconductors
item.description:
A semiconductor fab uses as much water as a small city and needs it cleaner than any city could make it. A single 300 millimetre wafer is rinsed in ultrapure water hundreds of times between the layers of circuits printed on it, and a large fab gets through thirty to fifty thousand cubic metres a day. The largest chipmaker's plants in Taiwan use around 150,000 cubic metres a day between them, the water of a city of half a million people.
In 2021 Taiwan's rain failed and the reservoirs that feed the science parks fell below ten percent. The government cut irrigation to seventy thousand hectares of rice paddy, paid the farmers, and sent water trucks to the fabs. The chips were made and the rice went unplanted. It was the clearest statement any country has made about what its water is for.
The industry has answered by recycling. The Taiwan fabs reuse about ninety percent of their water within the plant, and the new ones in Arizona and Japan are being built with reclaimed water and near zero discharge, because the places that want chips are the places with the least water to spare.
The long version is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Oil and Gas
item.description:
An oil well is mostly a water well. Oil sits in rock with ancient seawater, and as a field ages the water share of what comes up rises, so that worldwide the industry lifts about three barrels of water for every barrel of oil, and in old fields ten. It is called produced water, it is saltier than the sea and laced with oil, metals and sometimes radium, and almost all of it is pumped back underground.
The new wells add water at the front. A fracked well in the Permian basin is made by pumping fifteen to forty million litres of water and sand into the rock under pressure, and the volume per well has grown several times over in a decade as the wells got longer. In West Texas, a desert, that water comes from aquifers and, increasingly, from the produced water of older wells, cleaned enough to use again.
The water that comes back has to go somewhere, and where it went in Oklahoma was deep injection wells, so many and so fast that the state went from two earthquakes a year to nine hundred.
The long version is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Ammonia
item.description:
About half the nitrogen in the protein of every person alive passed through an ammonia plant. The Haber Bosch process takes hydrogen, mostly from natural gas, and nitrogen from the air, and joins them at high pressure into ammonia, which becomes urea, ammonium nitrate and the other fertilisers that doubled the world's food in a century. The world makes about 180 million tonnes of it a year.
Water is in the recipe. The hydrogen comes from splitting methane with steam, and about half of the hydrogen atoms in the ammonia came from water: roughly a tonne of water, as an ingredient, in every tonne of ammonia. The plant then needs many tonnes more to carry away the heat, which is why every ammonia plant is on a river, a coast or a large cooling tower.
The water that matters more is at the other end. Ammonia becomes fertiliser, fertiliser becomes nitrate, and nitrate is in the wells and rivers of every farming region on Earth, which is the story the nitrate article on this site tells. The plant's water is a footnote to the fertiliser's.
The long version is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Cannabis
item.description:
An outdoor cannabis plant in a California summer uses about twenty two litres of water a day, which is about twice what a grapevine on the same hillside takes. Over a season of a hundred and fifty days that is three thousand litres or more a plant, and a plant gives about half a kilogram to a kilogram of dried flower. Per kilogram the number is in the thousands of litres, which puts cannabis near beef and far above any vegetable, and per crop the number is tiny, because the crop is tiny.
The problem was never the total. It was where and when. Before legalisation the grows were in the forested hills of northern California, in the catchments of small streams that run low in summer, and the water was pumped straight out of them in August, when the salmon needed it most. A study of four watersheds in 2015 found grows taking more than the streams' entire summer flow.
Indoor growing uses less water and vastly more electricity: about one percent of the electricity in the United States goes to growing cannabis under lights. Legalisation brought permits, meters and tanks, and it moved the crop to farmland with rights to the water it uses.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Storm Overflows
item.description:
Most cities older than a century carry rain and sewage in the same pipe. The Victorian engineers who built the sewers had one pipe to lay and put everything in it, and they built overflows along it so that when a storm filled the pipe faster than the works could take it, the excess would go into the river rather than back up into the streets. The overflows still work. In England in 2023 they spilled for 3.6 million hours.
What comes out is rainwater mixed with sewage, diluted but untreated, and for a hundred years nobody counted it, because nobody was watching. From 2016 the overflows in England were fitted with monitors, by 2023 nearly all of them, and the count that resulted turned a plumbing detail into the largest environmental argument in the country.
The fix is storage: tanks and tunnels that hold the storm flow until the works can treat it. London's answer is a tunnel twenty five kilometres long under the Thames that cost about five billion pounds and opened in 2025. Every old city has the same sewers and most have not yet built the tunnel.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Myth: A Filter Jug Makes Tap Water Safer
item.description:
A filter jug does one thing well: it takes the chlorine out of tap water and with it the taste and smell that people dislike. It also takes out some of the hardness, a little lead and copper if the pipes are shedding them, and not much else. It does not remove nitrate, fluoride, most pesticides, PFAS, or bacteria and viruses, and the tests that back the claims on the box are tests of taste, not of safety.
The water that comes out of the jug can be less safe than the water that went in. The chlorine that the cartridge removes is what stops bacteria growing in the water, and the carbon it removes it with is a warm, wet, nutrient rich surface on which bacteria grow very well. Studies of jugs in ordinary kitchens have found bacterial counts in the filtered water many times those in the tap, especially after the four weeks the cartridge is supposed to last.
If the tap water meets the standard, the jug makes it taste better and that is all. If it does not, the jug is the wrong filter for almost every reason it might fail.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFacts #WaterEducation #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Wool
item.description:
A kilogram of clean wool carries about 17,000 litres of water in the global averages, which puts it above beef and far above cotton. A wool jumper, at four hundred grams, is about 7,000 litres. The number is enormous, and it is one of the least worrying on this site.
The reason is where the water is. A sheep is a grazing animal on land that is too steep, cold, dry or poor for a crop: the uplands of Britain and New Zealand, the outback of Australia, the plateaus of Patagonia. The rain that fell on that pasture, and that the grass drank and the sheep ate, is nearly the whole of the footprint, and it would have fallen there whether or not the sheep was standing on it. The blue share, water pumped for the sheep or the grass, is a few percent.
The water that matters is at the scouring plant, where raw fleece is washed of its grease, dirt and dung in hot water and detergent, and the effluent is among the strongest in the textile trade. And the alternative, acrylic, is polyester's cousin: sixty litres, made of oil, and shedding plastic in every wash.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Tomato
item.description:
A kilogram of tomatoes takes about 214 litres of water in the global averages, which makes it one of the least thirsty things on the shelf. The average hides a range of thirty to one. A tomato from a heated glasshouse in the Netherlands, grown on rockwool with the water recycled, takes under twenty litres a kilogram. A tomato from an open field in a dry region, flood irrigated, can take five hundred.
The reason is that a plant in a field loses most of its water to the air and the soil around it, and a plant in a closed greenhouse loses almost nothing. The Dutch have taken that to its limit, at a cost in gas and glass, and produce more tomatoes per hectare than anywhere on Earth. Most of the world's tomatoes are still grown in fields, in China, India, Turkey, Egypt, Italy, Spain and California, because fields are cheap, and the ones that go into paste and ketchup come from the driest of those places.
The tin of paste on the shelf is Central Valley groundwater, and the salad tomato is, increasingly, Dutch gas.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Potato
item.description:
A kilogram of potatoes takes about 290 litres of water to grow. Wheat takes 1,800, rice 2,500, and the difference is not the plant's thirst but its yield: a hectare of potatoes gives forty tonnes of food where a hectare of wheat gives four. Per calorie, per gram of protein and per kilogram, the potato is the least thirsty staple there is.
It is also mostly water itself, about eighty percent, which is why the number changes when the water is taken out. A kilogram of crisps is about four kilograms of potatoes, fried, so it carries a thousand litres and more, plus what the factory used to wash, peel, slice and rinse the starch off. A kilogram of frozen chips is somewhere in between.
The potato's water is mostly rain, in the cool climates where it grows best, and irrigation where it does not, on the sandy soils of Idaho, the Netherlands and the English fens. It is the crop a dry world should be growing more of, and in China and India, which now grow most of it, it is.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Melbourne
item.description:
Melbourne's water comes from forests. For over a century the city has closed the mountain catchments to the east to the public, so that the rain that falls on them runs through undisturbed eucalyptus into reservoirs that need almost no treatment. It is one of the cleanest supplies in the world, and in the Millennium Drought it nearly ran out.
The drought lasted from 1997 to 2009, the reservoirs fell to about a quarter, and the city did something this series rarely sees: it halved its use, from about 250 litres a person a day to under 150, without rota rationing, through a decade of restrictions, a campaign that asked for four minute showers and handed out timers, rebates for tanks and efficient fittings, and a tariff that rose with use. The habit stuck; the city's use never fully went back.
It also built a desalination plant that opened in 2012, after the rain returned, and did not order a drop of water from it for five years. The plant was called a white elephant until the dry years of 2019, when it was not.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Lagos
item.description:
Lagos has more water than almost any city in this series: two metres of rain a year, a lagoon, the Atlantic, and rivers on three sides. About one household in ten has a working tap. The rest drink from boreholes drilled under the house, from vendors pushing carts, and from sachets, half a litre of water sealed in a plastic bag and sold for a few naira on every corner.
The utility's treatment plants were built for a city of a million. Lagos has passed twenty million. The works run at a fraction of their capacity because the power fails, the pumps are old, and the pipes lose most of what they carry. So the city dug: several hundred thousand boreholes into an aquifer that is now salting from the sea and fouled from the pit latrines beside it.
The sachet is the answer the market found. It is cleaner than the borehole, cheaper than the vendor, and it produces a few billion plastic bags a year that block the drains the rain needs. Lagos floods with the water it cannot drink, and drinks the water it cannot afford.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Karachi
item.description:
Karachi has about twenty million people and a piped water system built for half that. On a good day the utility delivers around half of what the city needs, from the Indus a hundred kilometres away and a lake that a bad monsoon empties. The other half arrives in tankers.
The tanker business is the city's second water utility. Thousands of trucks fill from hydrants, legal ones that the utility runs and illegal ones tapped into the mains, and sell the water by the load to apartment blocks, factories and the settlements where the pipes never reached, at prices per litre that run ten to twenty times the piped tariff. The people who run the illegal hydrants have been called a mafia in the city's newspapers for twenty years, and the word is not an exaggeration.
The fix has been designed since the 1990s: a new bulk supply from the Indus, a repaired network, meters and a tariff. It has been approved, funded, started and stalled in every decade since, because the people who profit from the tankers include some of the people who would have to build it.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Cairo
item.description:
Egypt is the Nile. Ninety seven percent of the country's fresh water is the river, a hundred and ten million people live within a few kilometres of it, and nearly every drop that reaches them fell as rain in Ethiopia, which has just finished a dam across the Blue Nile that can hold more than a year of the river's flow.
The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam will not, once full, take much water from Egypt in a normal year; hydroelectric dams pass the water through. What it takes is control. For the first time since the pharaohs, the flow that reaches Egypt in a drought will be decided upstream, by a government Egypt has no treaty with, and the two countries have spent a decade failing to agree what that means.
Meanwhile the delta, where two thirds of Egypt's food grows, is sinking and salting as the Mediterranean pushes into land the river no longer builds, Cairo has grown to twenty million people on water shared with the farms, and the country has begun to do what every place in this series does when the river is spoken for: reuse its sewage, desalinate the coast, and line the canals.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Barcelona
item.description:
In May 2008 Barcelona was drinking from ships. The reservoirs of the Ter and Llobregat rivers, which supply five million people, had fallen to about a fifth, and the city hired tankers to bring fresh water from Marseille and Tarragona into the port, ten million litres a load, while it argued with the rest of Spain about a pipeline from the Ebro. The rain came in June and the ships stopped.
The city's answer was the sea. The El Prat desalination plant opened in 2009, the largest in Europe at the time, and for a decade it ran at a fraction of capacity because the rain came back and the water it made cost more than the river's. Then the drought of 2021 to 2024 arrived, longer and deeper than 2008, the reservoirs fell to fifteen percent, the plant ran flat out, Barcelona declared an emergency and cut its per person allowance, and the city came within weeks of a second round of ships.
It held, on desalination, on reused sewage sent into the river above the intakes, and on a public that cut its use to among the lowest in Europe. The lesson, learned twice, is that a plant built for a drought has to be run through the wet years too.
The long version is on the site.

item.title: Thirsty Places: Bangalore
item.description:
Bangalore, a city of fourteen million that runs a large share of the world's software, was built on a plateau with no river, on a landscape of hundreds of rain fed lakes that its founders dug in the sixteenth century to hold the monsoon. Over the last forty years the city drained most of the lakes, built its technology parks on their beds, and pumped the aquifer beneath them for the half of the city the pipes never reached.
In March 2024 the wells ran dry across the outer city, the tanker price tripled, the technology companies sent staff home, and the state banned the use of drinking water to wash cars. The piped supply, pumped 1,400 metres up from the Kaveri a hundred kilometres away, reaches the old city; the new one, the software corridor built on the lake beds, has no pipes and had, that summer, no water.
The lakes that remain make the news in their own way. Bellandur, the largest, catches fire, because the sewage and the chemicals that flow into it foam and burn. The fix is the one this series always finds: pipes to the whole city, sewage treated and returned, rain caught on roofs and in the lakes that are left. The city has started on all three.
The long version is on the site.

item.title: Thirsty: Palm Oil
item.description:
Palm oil has the worst reputation of any crop on the shelf and the smallest water footprint of any oil in the aisle. A kilogram of it takes about 5,000 litres, almost all rain, against 14,500 for olive oil and around 8,000 for rapeseed and sunflower. The oil palm is the most productive oil crop on Earth, and it grows where it rains every week.
So the water story is upside down. Nothing is pumped for it. What matters is what comes out of the mill: palm oil mill effluent, a hot brown soup of oil, fibre and sugar that carries a hundred times the organic load of sewage and that, in the districts of Sumatra and Borneo where the mills are, has turned rivers black. And what the plantations did to get their land, draining peat swamps that held the rain of a whole region and now burn every dry season.
Palm oil's water sits outside the oil: in the river below the mill and the swamp that used to be there.
The long version is on the site.

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Pharmaceuticals
item.description:
A pharmaceutical plant is a water plant with a drug factory attached. Before a tablet or an injection is made, the plant makes purified water, and, for anything that goes into a vein, water for injection, which is distilled or passed through membranes until it carries almost nothing, and then kept hot and moving so that nothing grows in it. The water is the ingredient that has to be perfect.
The outfall is the other end. A plant that makes antibiotics washes its vessels and loses a share of the product to the drain, and in the bulk drug districts of Hyderabad and Chennai, where much of the world's antibiotic supply is made, rivers and lakes below the plants have carried ciprofloxacin at concentrations higher than a patient's blood. That is where resistant bacteria are bred, in the water, by the tonne.
The drugs in a European or American river come from a different place: from people, through the sewage works, which removes some and passes the rest. The industry has learned, under pressure, to treat its own effluent. The sewage works is only now learning to treat ours.
The long version is on the site.

item.title: Thirsty: Cotton or Polyester
item.description:
A cotton t-shirt carries about 2,700 litres of water. A polyester one carries a few dozen. On the water footprint alone, the choice looks settled, and it is not, because the two fibres spend their water in different places and leave different things behind.
Cotton's water is a field: rain and irrigation on a crop that grows in hot, dry places, in Uzbekistan, India, Texas and Egypt, and that emptied the Aral Sea. Polyester's water is a refinery and a spinning line, a fraction of the volume, in places that mostly have it. On the water used, polyester wins by a mile.
Then the garment goes into a washing machine. Every wash of a polyester shirt sheds hundreds of thousands of plastic fibres that pass the sewage works into the sludge and the river. Cotton sheds cellulose, which rots. Polyester also comes from oil and lasts for centuries in a landfill. So the honest sentence is this: polyester is the better choice for water and the worse one for plastic, and the best choice is the shirt you keep for ten years, whichever it is made of.
The long version is on the site.

item.title: Thirsty: Car
item.description:
A car takes somewhere between fifty and four hundred thousand litres of water to build, depending on who counts and what they count. A middle figure is around 150,000. That is fifty years of a person's drinking water, for a machine that weighs a tonne and a half.
Most of it is in the materials. A tonne of steel keeps about 3,300 litres, and a car has most of a tonne. Aluminium is thirstier per kilogram, and so is the copper in the wiring and the rubber in the tyres. The paint shop, which most people never think of, is the single largest water user inside the assembly plant, because a body is washed, phosphated, dipped and rinsed a dozen times before the first coat.
An electric car changes where the water is spent rather than how much. It has no engine and no fuel to refine, and it has a battery whose lithium, nickel and cobalt come from brine ponds and mines in dry places. The number on the car is similar. The number on the map moves from the refinery to the Atacama.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Battery
item.description:
The battery in an electric car holds about eight kilograms of lithium. To get that lithium out of the salt flats of Chile and Argentina, where most of it comes from, about two million litres of brine are pumped up and left in ponds to evaporate for a year or more. Whether that counts as water is the argument.
The brine is salt water, several times saltier than the sea, from an aquifer nobody drinks. The industry says evaporating it uses no fresh water worth counting. The villages on the edges of the salars say the brine and the fresh water under the mountains are one system, that the lagoons have dropped and the springs have dried, and the hydrology is on their side more often than not.
Then there is the rest of the battery: nickel from Indonesia, cobalt from Congo, graphite from China, each with a mine and a refinery. And there are two things that change the picture: direct lithium extraction, which returns the brine to the ground, and recycling, which uses a fraction of the water of any mine. The battery's water is a number with a decision inside it.
The long version is on the site.

item.title: Plain Water: Tailings
item.description:
A mine grinds rock to powder, takes out the metal, and is left with the powder, wet. It pumps the slurry to a valley and builds a dam across the valley's mouth, and the dam is raised, year by year, out of the tailings themselves. There are several thousand such dams in the world, holding, between them, hundreds of cubic kilometres of ground rock and the water that carried it. Some are the largest structures humans have built.
The water is the danger. A tailings dam holds a slurry, and a slurry that is shaken, overtopped or built on too fast can turn back into a liquid in seconds and flow. At Brumadinho in Brazil in January 2019 that happened to an iron ore dam at lunchtime, and a wave of twelve million cubic metres of mud reached the mine's offices and canteen in minutes and killed 270 people. Four years earlier a dam a hundred kilometres away had buried a village and fouled a river to the sea.
Since then the industry has written a global standard and begun, at the newer mines, to filter the tailings and stack them dry, which removes the water and the risk at a cost the copper price can bear. The old dams are still there, thousands of them, raised out of mud, above towns.
The long version is on the site.

item.title: Plain Water: Nitrate
item.description:
Nitrate is the water problem that farming made. Every kilogram of nitrogen fertiliser that a crop does not take up, and a crop takes about half, dissolves in the rain and moves down through the soil into the groundwater, where it stays. A fifth of the wells in Europe's farming regions exceed the drinking water limit of fifty milligrams a litre, and the water arriving at those wells now fell as rain on fields fertilised in the 1990s.
At the limit and above, nitrate can starve a baby's blood of oxygen, the blue baby condition that set the limit in the first place, and it is under study for cancers of the gut in adults at lower doses. In a river or a bay it is the nitrogen article's algae. The treatment is ion exchange or reverse osmosis, expensive and permanent, and the cure is on the field: less fertiliser, applied when the crop can take it, with a cover crop to hold what is left.
Denmark cut its nitrate losses by half over thirty years. Most farming regions have not started, and the groundwater under them will carry this decade's fertiliser to the wells of the 2050s.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Lead
item.description:
There is no lead in the water that leaves a treatment plant. It gets in afterwards, from the pipe that runs from the main under the street to the house, which in most cities built before 1950 is made of lead, because lead was soft, cheap and easy to bend round a corner. Millions of those pipes are still in the ground: about nine million in the United States, and a large share of the connections in Britain, France and the older cities of Europe.
Whether the lead comes off depends on the water. A water with the right chemistry lays a film of scale inside the pipe that seals it. Change the water, as Flint did in 2014 when it switched to a more corrosive river and skipped the treatment that keeps the film, and the film dissolves and the lead follows, into the kettles of a hundred thousand people. Lead damages a child's brain at any dose that has been measured, which is why the guideline is zero and no city meets it.
The plant cannot fix it. The only fix is to dig up the pipe, and the countries that have started doing that will be finished around 2040.
The long version is on the site.

item.title: Plain Water: Cholera
item.description:
In 1854 a doctor in London named John Snow mapped the deaths in a cholera outbreak in Soho and found them clustered around one public pump on Broad Street. He persuaded the parish to take the handle off. The outbreak, already fading, ended, and the idea that a disease could travel in water rather than in bad air had its first piece of evidence. The pump's well, it turned out, was a metre from a leaking cesspit.
Thirty years later the bacterium was identified, and within a generation every city that could afford it had built what London built after its Great Stink: sewers to take the waste away and filtered, later chlorinated, water to bring the supply in. Cholera left those cities and has never come back.
It kills tens of thousands a year today, in Yemen, Haiti, Sudan, the Congo and the camps of every war and flood, where the supply is a river that the sewage runs into. It is curable with a bag of salt and sugar in clean water, and it is prevented with a treatment plant and a sewer, which is the whole of this site in one disease.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Myth: A Lawn Is Harmless
item.description:
A lawn is a crop. Turf grass covers more land in the United States than corn, about 160,000 square kilometres, and it is the largest irrigated crop in the country. It just does not get harvested.
In a wet climate a lawn is fine: the rain waters it and the water it uses would have gone into the ground anyway. In a hot dry one, which is where most of the world's suburbs have been built in the last fifty years, a green lawn needs about a bath of water a week for every ten square metres, sprayed on in the evening so that a share of it evaporates before it reaches a root. In Las Vegas, Phoenix, Los Angeles, Perth, Riyadh and Dubai, outdoor watering is half or more of a household's use, and the lawn is most of the outdoor.
Las Vegas paid its residents to dig theirs up, then banned the ornamental kind by law. The grass had to go because it was the only water the city really lost: a shower goes back to the treatment plant, a sprinkler goes into the sky.
The long version is on the site.

item.title: Myth: Washing Up by Hand Saves Water
item.description:
A modern dishwasher uses about ten litres of water for a full load, twelve place settings, and heats it to sixty degrees. A person washing the same dishes by hand under a running tap uses somewhere between forty and a hundred, and the studies that have measured people at real sinks put the average nearer the top. The machine wins by a factor of four to ten.
It wins because it washes the same small volume over and over: a pump sprays a few litres round the cabinet for an hour, the water is filtered and sprayed again, and only at the end is it drained and replaced. A tap does not recycle. It runs at six to ten litres a minute into a sink whose water goes straight to the drain.
Washing up in a bowl, with the tap off, is a different story: fifteen or twenty litres, close to the machine, if the rinse is done in a second bowl rather than under the tap. The myth is that the machine is the wasteful option. The waste, in the kitchen as in the bathroom, is the running tap.
